claim: Breast cancer had 287,850 new cases in 2022 in the United States.
source: Breast cancer (BC) is a fatal disease with 287,850 new cases in 2022 in the United States and an estimated mortality rate of 43,250 (https://seer.cancer.gov/statfacts/html/breast.html).
evidence: The claim cites a specific data source (SEER cancer statistics website) for the number of new breast cancer cases.

claim: Breast cancer had an estimated mortality rate of 43,250 in 2022 in the United States.
source: Breast cancer (BC) is a fatal disease with 287,850 new cases in 2022 in the United States and an estimated mortality rate of 43,250 (https://seer.cancer.gov/statfacts/html/breast.html).
evidence: The claim cites a specific data source (SEER cancer statistics website) for breast cancer mortality.

claim: HR+/HER2- breast cancer accounts for 68% of all breast cancer cases.
source: The most common BC subtype is positive for hormone receptor (HR+) and does not overexpress the human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2/neu), accounting for 68% of all BC cases (https://seer.cancer.gov/statfacts/html/breast-subtypes.html).
evidence: The claim cites a specific data source (SEER cancer statistics website) for the prevalence of this breast cancer subtype.

claim: Resistance to estrogen signaling therapies in metastatic breast cancer is a significant challenge.
source: The primary treatment for estrogen receptor positive (ER+), HER2− BC are therapies targeting estrogen signaling; however, resistance to these therapies in metastatic BC (mBC) and disease progression remains a significant challenge (Osborne and Schiff, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Aberrant activation of mTOR signaling has been identified in multiple human tumors.
source: Aberrant activation of the mammalian (mechanistic) target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling has been identified in multiple human tumors (Hare and Harvey, 2017; Ortolani et al., 2015) and is involved in resistance to endocrine therapy (Johnston, 2015; Osborne and Schiff, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: mTOR signaling is involved in resistance to endocrine therapy.
source: Aberrant activation of the mammalian (mechanistic) target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling has been identified in multiple human tumors (Hare and Harvey, 2017; Ortolani et al., 2015) and is involved in resistance to endocrine therapy (Johnston, 2015; Osborne and Schiff, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Everolimus binds to FKBP-12 to generate a complex that inhibits mTOR activation.
source: Everolimus, an analog of rapamycin, binds to the immunophilin FK Binding Protein-12 (FKBP-12) to generate a complex that inhibits the activation of mTOR, a key regulatory kinase (Faivre et al., 2006; Law et al., 2006; Mita et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature describing the mechanism of everolimus.

claim: Everolimus in combination with exemestane improved progression-free survival in patients with advanced breast cancer.
source: Everolimus in combination with the aromatase inhibitor exemestane improved progression-free survival in patients with advanced BC (Baselga et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a clinical study.

claim: The combination of everolimus and exemestane was approved in 2012 as a second-line therapy for recurrent or metastatic breast cancer.
source: Based on these clinical studies the combination was approved in 2012 as a second-line therapy for recurrent or mBC (National Comprehensive Cancer Network, NCCN guidelines) (Baselga et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to NCCN guidelines and a citation to the clinical study that led to approval.

claim: A large subset of patients develops progression and resistance to everolimus and exemestane combination therapy.
source: Despite its efficacy, a large subset of patients develops progression and resistance to this combination, highlighting the need for more effective therapeutic strategies for advanced BC.
evidence: The claim is based on established clinical knowledge about treatment resistance.

claim: Everolimus resistance in breast cancer involves activation of AKT signaling.
source: Studies on everolimus resistance in BC revealed survival mechanisms including activation of Protein kinase B family (AKT) (Carew et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013) and Mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling (Campone et al., 2021; Carew et al., 2011; Kimura et al., 2018; Mendoza et al., 2011), upregulation of MYC (Bihani et al., 2015; Lui et al., 2016), increased oxidative stress (Neklesa and Davis, 2008), metabolic reprogramming (Pusapati et al., 2016), increased expression of anti-apoptotic molecules such as survivin (Taglieri et al., 2017), and activation of epithelial and mesenchymal transition (Holder et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on everolimus resistance mechanisms.

claim: Everolimus resistance in breast cancer involves activation of MAPK signaling.
source: Studies on everolimus resistance in BC revealed survival mechanisms including activation of Protein kinase B family (AKT) (Carew et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013) and Mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling (Campone et al., 2021; Carew et al., 2011; Kimura et al., 2018; Mendoza et al., 2011), upregulation of MYC (Bihani et al., 2015; Lui et al., 2016), increased oxidative stress (Neklesa and Davis, 2008), metabolic reprogramming (Pusapati et al., 2016), increased expression of anti-apoptotic molecules such as survivin (Taglieri et al., 2017), and activation of epithelial and mesenchymal transition (Holder et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on everolimus resistance mechanisms.

source: Studies on everolimus resistance in BC revealed survival mechanisms including activation of Protein kinase B family (AKT) (Carew et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013) and Mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling (Campone et al., 2021; Carew et al., 2011; Kimura et al., 2018; Mendoza et al., 2011), upregulation of MYC (Bihani et al., 2015; Lui et al., 2016), increased oxidative stress (Neklesa and Davis, 2008), metabolic reprogramming (Pusapati et al., 2016), increased expression of anti-apoptotic molecules such as survivin (Taglieri et al., 2017), and activation of epithelial and mesenchymal transition (Holder et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on everolimus resistance mechanisms.

claim: Everolimus resistance in breast cancer involves increased oxidative stress.
source: Studies on everolimus resistance in BC revealed survival mechanisms including activation of Protein kinase B family (AKT) (Carew et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013) and Mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling (Campone et al., 2021; Carew et al., 2011; Kimura et al., 2018; Mendoza et al., 2011), upregulation of MYC (Bihani et al., 2015; Lui et al., 2016), increased oxidative stress (Neklesa and Davis, 2008), metabolic reprogramming (Pusapati et al., 2016), increased expression of anti-apoptotic molecules such as survivin (Taglieri et al., 2017), and activation of epithelial and mesenchymal transition (Holder et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on everolimus resistance mechanisms.

source: Studies on everolimus resistance in BC revealed survival mechanisms including activation of Protein kinase B family (AKT) (Carew et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013) and Mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling (Campone et al., 2021; Carew et al., 2011; Kimura et al., 2018; Mendoza et al., 2011), upregulation of MYC (Bihani et al., 2015; Lui et al., 2016), increased oxidative stress (Neklesa and Davis, 2008), metabolic reprogramming (Pusapati et al., 2016), increased expression of anti-apoptotic molecules such as survivin (Taglieri et al., 2017), and activation of epithelial and mesenchymal transition (Holder et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on everolimus resistance mechanisms.

claim: Everolimus resistance in breast cancer involves increased expression of survivin.
source: Studies on everolimus resistance in BC revealed survival mechanisms including activation of Protein kinase B family (AKT) (Carew et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013) and Mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling (Campone et al., 2021; Carew et al., 2011; Kimura et al., 2018; Mendoza et al., 2011), upregulation of MYC (Bihani et al., 2015; Lui et al., 2016), increased oxidative stress (Neklesa and Davis, 2008), metabolic reprogramming (Pusapati et al., 2016), increased expression of anti-apoptotic molecules such as survivin (Taglieri et al., 2017), and activation of epithelial and mesenchymal transition (Holder et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on everolimus resistance mechanisms.

claim: Everolimus resistance in breast cancer involves activation of epithelial and mesenchymal transition.
source: Studies on everolimus resistance in BC revealed survival mechanisms including activation of Protein kinase B family (AKT) (Carew et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2013) and Mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling (Campone et al., 2021; Carew et al., 2011; Kimura et al., 2018; Mendoza et al., 2011), upregulation of MYC (Bihani et al., 2015; Lui et al., 2016), increased oxidative stress (Neklesa and Davis, 2008), metabolic reprogramming (Pusapati et al., 2016), increased expression of anti-apoptotic molecules such as survivin (Taglieri et al., 2017), and activation of epithelial and mesenchymal transition (Holder et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on everolimus resistance mechanisms.

claim: ONC201/TIC10 is currently being evaluated in clinical trials for solid tumors including breast and endometrial cancer, gliomas, and hematological malignancies.
source: ONC201/TIC10 belongs to the imipridone class of inhibitors and is currently being evaluated in clinical trials for solid tumors including breast and endometrial cancer, gliomas, and hematological malignancies (Prabhu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review article about ONC201/TIC10 clinical trials.

claim: ONC201/TIC10 mechanism involves binding and activation of mitochondrial protease ClpP.
source: The mechanism of ONC201/TIC10 action involves binding and activation of the mitochondrial protease caseinolytic protease P (ClpP) (Greer et al., 2022; Jacques et al., 2020; Graves et al., 2019; Ishizawa et al., 2019) and inhibition of the G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) dopamine receptor D2 (DRD2) (Kline et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies on ONC201/TIC10 mechanism.

claim: ONC201/TIC10 mechanism involves inhibition of dopamine receptor D2 (DRD2).
source: The mechanism of ONC201/TIC10 action involves binding and activation of the mitochondrial protease caseinolytic protease P (ClpP) (Greer et al., 2022; Jacques et al., 2020; Graves et al., 2019; Ishizawa et al., 2019) and inhibition of the G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) dopamine receptor D2 (DRD2) (Kline et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study on ONC201/TIC10 mechanism.

claim: ONC201/TIC10 synergizes with everolimus in prostate cancer.
source: ONC201/TIC10 has been shown to synergize with everolimus in prostate cancer (Lev et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Colorectal cancer cells were more sensitive to the combination of ONC201/TIC10 with mTOR inhibitor AZD-8055.
source: Furthermore, colorectal cancer cells were more sensitive to the combination of ONC201/TIC10 with mTOR inhibitor AZD-8055 (Jin et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Upregulation of mitochondrial ClpP has been reported in breast cancer cells and tissues.
source: While the effectiveness of the combination of everolimus with ONC201/TIC10 has not been studied in BC, upregulation of mitochondrial ClpP that is a target of ONC201/TIC10 has been reported both in BC cells and tissues (Cormio et al., 2021; Luo et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: ONC201/TIC10 inhibits mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation in breast cancer cells, causing depletion of cellular ATP.
source: In addition, ONC201/TIC10 inhibits mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation in BC cells, causing depletion of cellular ATP (Dwucet et al., 2021; Greer et al., 2018; Ishida et al., 2018; Pruss et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Increased dependency on oxidative phosphorylation has been shown in chemotherapy resistant triple negative breast cancer.
source: Increased dependency on oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) has been shown in chemotherapy resistant triple negative BC (Evans et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Everolimus resistant cell lines were generated by long-term culture of parental cell lines in the continuous presence of 100 nM everolimus for MCF7 and T47D or 50 nM everolimus for CAMA-1 for 6–12 months.
source: Everolimus resistant cell lines were generated by long-term culture of parental cell lines in the continuous presence of 100 nM everolimus for MCF7 and T47D or 50 nM everolimus for CAMA-1 for 6–12 months (McDermott et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim describes the experimental method used to generate resistant cell lines, with citation to a similar methodology.

claim: Resistant cells showed a statistically significant reduced response to everolimus compared to sensitive cells (p < 0.05 for all paired cell lines).
source: Resistant cells showed a statistically significant reduced response to everolimus compared to sensitive cells (p < 0.05 for all paired cell lines, Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A with statistical analysis.

claim: ONC201/TIC10 single agent inhibited the proliferation of CAMA-1, MCF7, and T47D sensitive and resistant cells in a dose-dependent manner with IC50 values ranging from 1.43 to 1.90 µM.
source: In the 2D assays, ONC201/TIC10 single agent inhibited the proliferation of CAMA-1, MCF7, and T47D sensitive and resistant cells in a dose-dependent manner with IC50 values ranging from 1.43 to 1.90 µM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ONC201/TIC10 single agent treatment resulted in significant growth inhibition compared to control and everolimus single agent in all the resistant cell lines and in the CAMA-1 and MCF7 sensitive cells.
source: ONC201/TIC10 single agent treatment resulted in significant growth inhibition compared to control and everolimus single agent in all the resistant cell lines and in the CAMA-1 and MCF7 sensitive cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Combination of ONC201/TIC10 with everolimus significantly decreased cell proliferation compared to ONC201/TIC10 single agent in all the resistant cell lines and in the MCF7 and T47D sensitive cells.
source: Combination of ONC201/TIC10 with everolimus significantly decreased cell proliferation compared to ONC201/TIC10 single agent, in all the resistant cell lines and in the MCF7 and T47D sensitive cells, by approximately 3% decrease for CAMA-1 sensitive, 5.5% for CAMA-1 resistant, 8% for MCF7 sensitive, 5% for MCF7 resistant, 8.8% for T74D sensitive, and 4.7% for T47D resistant (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B with quantitative measurements.

claim: Analysis of the drug interactions using the Bliss Interaction Index showed additive effect in all sensitive cell lines and T47D resistant cells and synergistic effect in the CAMA-1 and MCF7 resistant cells in 2D assays.
source: Analysis of the drug interactions using the Bliss Interaction Index showed additive effect in all sensitive cell lines and T47D resistant cells and synergistic effect in the CAMA-1 and MCF7 resistant cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by drug interaction analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In 3D assays, ONC201/TIC10 single agent treatment resulted in significant growth inhibition compared to control in all the resistant cell lines and in the T47D sensitive cells.
source: In the 3D assays, ONC201/TIC10 single agent treatment resulted in significant growth inhibition compared to control in the all the resistant cell lines and in the T47D sensitive cells as indicated by the fluorescence intensity (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: In 3D assays, the combination of ONC201/TIC10 with everolimus significantly inhibited spheroid growth in sensitive and resistant cell lines compared to both everolimus and ONC201/TIC10 single agent.
source: Even though everolimus single agent had increased inhibitory effect compared to ONC201/TIC10 single agent, the combination significantly inhibited spheroid growth in sensitive and resistant cell lines compared to both everolimus and ONC201/TIC10 single agent (Figure 2A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: Drug interactions analysis in 3D assays showed moderately better than additive effect in the CAMA-1 resistant cells as well as in T47D sensitive and resistant cells.
source: Drug interactions analysis showed moderately better than additive effect in the CAMA-1 resistant cells as well as in T47D sensitive and resistant cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by drug interaction analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Combination therapy of ONC201/TIC10 with everolimus inhibits spheroid growth of primary patient-derived ER+ BC cells compared to everolimus single agent or ONC201/TIC10 single agent.
source: Our results indicate that combination therapy of ONC201/TIC10 with everolimus inhibits spheroid growth compared to everolimus single agent or ONC201/TIC10 single agent (ONC201/TIC10 single agent vs. combination 12.5% cell proliferation decrease for P1, 11% for P2, 4% for P3, 0.2% for P4, and 10.5% for P5) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from primary patient cells shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ONC201/TIC10 single agent or combination of ONC201/TIC10 with everolimus exhibited greater growth inhibition in post-everolimus treatment cells compared to cells acquired during everolimus treatment.
source: ONC201/TIC10 single agent or combination of ONC201/TIC10 with everolimus exhibited greater growth inhibition in the post-everolimus treatment cells (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) as shown by the significant reduction in proliferation of these cells compared to the cells acquired during everolimus treatment (7.2% cell decrease in cell proliferation during everolimus vs. post-everolimus with ONC201/TIC10 and 9.2% cell decrease in cell proliferation during everolimus vs. post-everolimus with the combination) (Figure 3B) and decreased spheroid size (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from patient P2 cells at different treatment time points shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ONC201/TIC10 suppresses the expression of mitochondrial proteins TFAM and TUFM in all sensitive and resistant cell lines.
source: Western blot analysis showed that ONC201/TIC10 suppresses the expression of the mitochondrial proteins TFAM (mitochondrial transcription factor A) and TUFM (translation elongation factor Tu) in all sensitive and resistant cell lines and specifically in a dose-dependent manner in CAMA-1 and T47D sensitive and resistant cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: TFAM and TUFM are important regulators of mitochondrial functions and are associated with ONC201/TIC10-induced mitochondrial disruption.
source: TFAM and TUFM are important regulators of mitochondrial functions and are associated with the ONC201/TIC10-induced mitochondrial disruption (Graves et al., 2019; Greer et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: ONC201/TIC10 suppresses the expression of respiratory chain complexes in sensitive and resistant cells, specifically Complex I subunit NDUFB8, Complex II subunit 30 kDa (CAMA-1 and MCF7), Complex III subunit Core 2, and ATP synthase subunit alpha.
source: ONC201/TIC10 suppresses the expression of the respiratory chain complexes in sensitive and resistant cells, specifically Complex I subunit NDUFB8, Complex II subunit 30 kDa (CAMA-1 and MCF7), Complex III subunit Core 2, and ATP synthase subunit alpha (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ONC201/TIC10 induces the expression of the chaperone BiP in all sensitive cell lines, and specifically in a dose-dependent manner in CAMA-1 and T47D sensitive and resistant cells.
source: ONC201/TIC10 induces the expression of the chaperone BiP (HP70) in all sensitive cell lines, and specifically in a dose-dependent manner in CAMA-1 and T47D sensitive and resistant cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ONC201/TIC10 induces the expression of the transcription factor ATF4 in all sensitive and resistant cell lines, with a dose-dependent effect in CAMA-1 and T47D sensitive cells.
source: Furthermore, ONC201/TIC10 induces the expression of the transcription factor ATF4 in all sensitive and resistant cell lines, with a dose-dependent effect in CAMA-1 and T47D sensitive cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The transcription factor CHOP is induced after ONC201/TIC10 treatment in all sensitive and resistant cell lines, with a dose-dependent effect in MCF7 and T47D sensitive and resistant cells.
source: The transcription factor CHOP is induced after treatment in all sensitive and resistant cell lines, with a dose-dependent effect in MCF7 and T47D sensitive and resistant cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Combination treatment of ONC201/TIC10 with everolimus had the same effect on the suppression of the mitochondrial proteins TFAM and TUFM and the OXPHOS complexes as the single agent.
source: Combination treatment of ONC201/TIC10 with everolimus had the same effect on the suppression of the mitochondrial proteins TFAM and TUFM and the OXPHOS complexes as the single agent (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Everolimus single agent did not affect the mitochondrial protein levels.
source: Everolimus single agent did not affect the mitochondrial protein levels, as expected (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Activation of stress response was not observed with the combination of ONC201/TIC10 and everolimus in the sensitive cells.
source: Activation of stress response was not observed with the combination in the sensitive cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Inhibition of AKT, ERK, and FoxO3a phosphorylation and activation of TRAIL were not observed in the everolimus sensitive and resistant cell model system.
source: Inhibition of AKT, ERK, and FoxO3a phosphorylation and activation of TRAIL that were previously described for ONC201/TIC10 (Allen et al., 2013; Ralff et al., 2017) were not observed in our model system (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and contrasts with previously published findings.

claim: ONC201/TIC10 inhibits the phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6 and this inhibition is increased in the resistant cell lines.
source: Furthermore, ONC201/TIC10 inhibits the phosphorylation of ribosomal protein S6 that is downstream of mTOR signaling and this inhibition is increased in the resistant cell lines (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: ONC201/TIC10 treatment significantly reduced cell cycle pathway activity in MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cell line over time (p = 1.8 × 10−6).
source: Over the time course, ONC201/TIC10 treatment significantly reduced cell cycle pathway activity in the cell line (p = 1.8 × 10−6) (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis of published data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ONC201/TIC10 treatment significantly increased ATF4 target genes activated in response to ER stress in MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cell line (p = 1.2 × 10−4).
source: Concurrently, we found a significant increase in the ATF4 target genes activated in response to ER stress (p = 1.2 × 10−4) (Figure 5B) and the UPR pathway activity (p = 1.8 × 10−4) (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis of published data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ONC201/TIC10 treatment significantly increased UPR pathway activity in MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cell line (p = 1.8 × 10−4).
source: Concurrently, we found a significant increase in the ATF4 target genes activated in response to ER stress (p = 1.2 × 10−4) (Figure 5B) and the UPR pathway activity (p = 1.8 × 10−4) (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis of published data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ERK signaling pathway showed no change in activity over time in MDA-MB-231 cells treated with ONC201/TIC10 (p = 0.55).
source: In contrast, neither of the ERK (p = 0.55) (Figure 5D) or AKT (p = 0.61) (Figure 5E) signaling pathways showed any change in activity over time.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis of published data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: AKT signaling pathway showed no change in activity over time in MDA-MB-231 cells treated with ONC201/TIC10 (p = 0.61).
source: In contrast, neither of the ERK (p = 0.55) (Figure 5D) or AKT (p = 0.61) (Figure 5E) signaling pathways showed any change in activity over time.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis of published data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CAMA-1 resistant cells have lower basal and maximal respiratory capacity compared to the sensitive cells.
source: Comparison of the mitochondrial respiration between the sensitive and resistant cells indicates that CAMA-1 resistant cells have lower basal and maximal respiratory capacity compared to the sensitive cells while MCF7 and T47D resistant cells have significantly increased baseline, maximal and ATP-linked respiration compared to the sensitive cells suggesting increased dependency on OXPHOS for ATP production (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by mitochondrial respiration data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: MCF7 and T47D resistant cells have significantly increased baseline, maximal and ATP-linked respiration compared to the sensitive cells suggesting increased dependency on OXPHOS for ATP production.
source: Comparison of the mitochondrial respiration between the sensitive and resistant cells indicates that CAMA-1 resistant cells have lower basal and maximal respiratory capacity compared to the sensitive cells while MCF7 and T47D resistant cells have significantly increased baseline, maximal and ATP-linked respiration compared to the sensitive cells suggesting increased dependency on OXPHOS for ATP production (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by mitochondrial respiration data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and includes an inference about OXPHOS dependency.

claim: All resistant cell lines showed significantly increased baseline and stressed extracellular acidification rate (ECAR).
source: Furthermore, all resistant lines showed significantly increased baseline and stressed extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ECAR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with ONC201/TIC10 resulted in a significant decrease in oxidative consumption rates (OCR) compared to control and everolimus single agent, in both sensitive and resistant cell lines at baseline, maximal and ATP-linked respiration.
source: Treatment with ONC201/TIC10 resulted in a significant decrease in oxidative consumption rates (OCR) compared to control and everolimus single agent, in both sensitive and resistant cell lines at baseline, maximal and ATP-linked respiration (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by OCR data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Combination treatment of ONC201/TIC10 with everolimus further reduced mitochondrial respiratory capacities in all sensitive and resistant cells, except CAMA-1 cells.
source: In addition, combination treatment of ONC201/TIC10 with everolimus further reduced mitochondrial respiratory capacities in all sensitive and resistant cells, except CAMA-1 cells that ONC201/TIC10 alone has similar effect on OCR as the combination (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by OCR data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Patients classified as everolimus responders based on decrease in Ki67 staining post-treatment displayed significant decrease in cell cycle signature (p = 4.3 × 10−3).
source: Patients classified as everolimus responders based on decrease in Ki67 staining post-treatment displayed significant decrease in cell cycle signature (p = 4.3 × 10−3), while non-responders did not show a significant change (p = 0.2) (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis of clinical trial data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Everolimus non-responders did not show a significant change in cell cycle signature (p = 0.2).
source: Patients classified as everolimus responders based on decrease in Ki67 staining post-treatment displayed significant decrease in cell cycle signature (p = 4.3 × 10−3), while non-responders did not show a significant change (p = 0.2) (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis of clinical trial data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: In the everolimus responder group, everolimus treatment led to a significant decrease in mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (p = 7.6 × 10−3).
source: In the responder group, we found that everolimus treatment led to a significant decrease in the mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (p = 7.6 × 10−3), while there was no significant difference in the non-responders' group (p = 0.83) (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis of clinical trial data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In the everolimus non-responders' group, there was no significant difference in mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (p = 0.83).
source: In the responder group, we found that everolimus treatment led to a significant decrease in the mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (p = 7.6 × 10−3), while there was no significant difference in the non-responders' group (p = 0.83) (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression analysis of clinical trial data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The BOLERO-2 study showed that addition of everolimus to exemestane significantly improves progression-free survival in post-menopausal ER+ breast cancers from 2.8 months on exemestane alone to 6.9 months on everolimus plus exemestane.
source: The BOLERO-2 study showed that addition of everolimus to exemestane significantly improves progression-free survival, in post-menopausal ER+ BCs from 2.8 months on exemestane alone to 6.9 months on everolimus plus exemestane (Baselga et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the BOLERO-2 clinical trial.

claim: ONC201/TIC10 was effective in TNBC cells in previous studies.
source: Previous studies showed the efficacy of ONC201/TIC10 in TNBC cells (Greer et al., 2018; Yuan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Non-responsive tumors continued to proliferate after everolimus treatment by utilizing oxidative phosphorylation pathway to fuel the growth of tumor cells.
source: Our results show that non-responsive tumors continued to proliferate after everolimus treatment by utilizing oxidative phosphorylation pathway to fuel the growth of tumor cells and is consistent with the findings from the resistant cell lines, supporting that ONC201/TIC10 and modulation of mitochondrial function is effective in drug resistant cancer cells.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' interpretation of their results from patient tumor data and resistant cell lines.

claim: Combination therapy with ONC201/TIC10 and everolimus showed increased growth inhibition in everolimus resistant breast cancer cell lines as well as resistant patient tumor cells in 2D and 3D studies.
source: Combination therapy with ONC201/TIC10 and everolimus showed increased growth inhibition in everolimus resistant BC cell lines as well as resistant patient tumor cells in 2D and 3D studies.
evidence: The claim summarizes experimental findings from multiple assays described in the manuscript.

claim: In 2D culture setting, ONC201/TIC10 was effective both as single agent and in combination with everolimus with similar potency in sensitive and resistant cells.
source: In the 2D culture setting, ONC201/TIC10 was effective both as single agent and in combination with everolimus with similar potency in sensitive and resistant cells.
evidence: The claim summarizes experimental findings from 2D assays.

claim: In 3D setting, ONC201/TIC10 in combination with everolimus had a robust effect on growth inhibition in both resistant and sensitive cells, compared to ONC201/TIC10 single agent that had a minor effect.
